statement:
Using the substitution $x=\alpha\cos^2\theta+\beta\sin^2\theta$, show that, if $\alpha<\beta$,
$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)}}\,dx=\pi.$$
What is the value of the above integral if $\alpha>\beta$?

Show also that, if $0<\alpha<\beta$,
$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\frac{1}{x\sqrt{(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}.$$
solution:
**First integral.** With $x=\alpha\cos^2\theta+\beta\sin^2\theta$,
$$x-\alpha=(\beta-\alpha)\sin^2\theta, \qquad \beta-x=(\beta-\alpha)\cos^2\theta,$$
so $\sqrt{(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)}=(\beta-\alpha)\sin\theta\cos\theta$ (all positive for $0<\theta<\pi/2$), and
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta}=2(\beta-\alpha)\sin\theta\cos\theta.$$
As $x$ goes from $\alpha$ to $\beta$, $\theta$ goes from $0$ to $\pi/2$. Hence
$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)}}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{2(\beta-\alpha)\sin\theta\cos\theta}{(\beta-\alpha)\sin\theta\cos\theta}\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}2\,d\theta=\pi.$$

If $\alpha>\beta$, the interval is traversed in the opposite direction, so the integral is $-\pi$.

**Second integral.** Use the same substitution. Since $x=\alpha\cos^2\theta+\beta\sin^2\theta$,
$$\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)}}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{2\,d\theta}{\alpha\cos^2\theta+\beta\sin^2\theta}.$$
Dividing top and bottom by $\cos^2\theta$,
$$=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sec^2\theta\,d\theta}{\alpha+\beta\tan^2\theta}.$$
Let $u=\tan\theta$, so $du=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $u$ goes from $0$ to $\infty$:
$$=2\int_0^{\infty}\frac{du}{\alpha+\beta u^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(u\sqrt{\frac\beta\alpha}\right)\right]_0^{\infty}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}\cdot\frac\pi2=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}}.$$
hints: Compute x-α and β-x under the substitution to simplify the square root.
The first integral reduces to ∫ 2 dθ over [0, π/2].
For the second, divide by cos²θ and substitute u = tan θ.
